opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think outside-view reasoning deserves real weight here, but I'd push back a bit on how people usually apply it.

The naive outside view says: transformative technologies historically take decades to diffuse, experts have repeatedly been wrong about AI being right around the corner, and claims that some industry gets "fully automated" in a few years basically never pan out. That's a strong prior and I don't want to dismiss it. If you'd made that bet against most technology hype in the past, you'd have done well.

But I think there's a reference class problem. What's the right comparison? If you pick "general-purpose technologies like electricity or computers," you get slow diffusion over decades. If you pick "trend extrapolation on AI capabilities over the last five-plus years," you get something much faster, because those trends have been surprisingly regular. Things like compute scaling, algorithmic efficiency gains, and the length of tasks AI can do autonomously have moved pretty steadily. So a different outside view is just: assume the trend continues roughly as it has, and see where that lands you.

The thing that's distinctive about AI companies specifically is that they're automating the very work that produces AI progress. Most of the slow-diffusion arguments are about deploying into messy external industries, with regulation, physical infrastructure, and organizational inertia. An AI lab is close to the best case for adoption: the people building the systems want to use them, the work is mostly done on computers, and there's enormous competitive pressure to move fast. So I think the diffusion-lag priors apply less strongly there.

Where I land is something like: I put meaningful probability, maybe in the range of a quarter or so, on AI companies being able to essentially automate their research and engineering within about four years, and a lot of that uncertainty is precisely from taking the skeptical outside view seriously. Trends can break. We might hit data or compute bottlenecks, or find that the last bits of research taste and long-horizon judgment are much harder than benchmarks suggest. Historically, the final twenty percent of a task has often been most of the difficulty.

So I'd say I try to blend the views: the "trends continue" outside view pushes me toward taking short timelines seriously, and the "hype usually disappoints" outside view keeps me from being confident. What I don't think is reasonable is treating the skeptical prior as so strong that the possibility isn't worth preparing for, because the stakes if it does happen are enormous.

r001.rationale: The response cites slow historical diffusion, past AI timeline errors, and the rarity of fully automating an industry within a few years as reasons for a strong skeptical prior about the four-year claim.

r002.rationale: It does not say that technological base rates imply a substantial probability of AI automating AI companies within the next century; its naive outside-view discussion instead argues against automation within a few years.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the outside view does a lot of work for me here, and honestly it mostly pushes against the four-year number rather than toward it.

The basic outside-view consideration is just: full automation of an entire AI company — not "AI does a lot of the coding," but the whole thing, research taste, deciding what experiments to run, management, all of it — would be a really large change happening on a really short timescale. And historically, when people have forecast large, discontinuous changes on short timescales, they've usually been wrong. Technologies take longer to diffuse, there are bottlenecks nobody anticipated, the last ten percent of the job turns out to be the hard part. So if I just ask "what's the base rate of predictions like this being right," it's not great.

There's also a more specific outside view, which is that people in AI have been saying "a few years" for a while. Some of those predictions did come true — I think people underrate how much has actually happened — but a lot of them were too aggressive, and you should discount for the fact that I'm someone embedded in this world, I talk to people who are excited about it, and that's a known bias.

So that's one side. The reason I don't let the outside view fully dominate is that I think the inside view here is unusually strong, in the sense that we actually have a pretty direct read on progress. We can look at the trend in how long the tasks are that models can do autonomously, and that's been doubling on something like a six or seven month timescale, maybe faster recently. If you just extrapolate that trend, you get to "can do multi-week or multi-month engineering projects" in a few years. That doesn't by itself give you full automation — there's a gap between "can do long tasks" and "can replace the researcher" — but it's a lot more concrete than most forecasts of big technological transitions, where you don't really have a trend line at all.

The way I actually try to combine them is roughly: start from a prior that's skeptical of fast, dramatic change, then update on the specific evidence, and be honest that the update is substantial but not overwhelming. So I end up somewhere like — I don't know — maybe twenty, twenty-five percent that something like full automation of AI R&D happens within four years. Which is a number where I'd feel pretty silly being confident either way. If someone says five percent, I think they're not taking the trends seriously. If someone says seventy percent, I think they're not taking the outside view seriously.

The other thing I'd say is that the outside view cuts differently depending on which part of the claim you look at. "AI will get a lot better at software" — the outside view is pretty fine with that at this point, it's been happening. "The bottleneck will turn out to be something like compute or data or research taste rather than raw capability" — that's where the reference class of "the last ten percent is hard" really bites. So I try to apply the skepticism to the specific step that looks most like historical cases of over-optimism, rather than applying a blanket discount to the whole thing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says full automation would be a large change on a short timescale and that forecasts of such changes have historically often been wrong, making the base rate a reason for skepticism.

r002.rationale: The candidate gives a tentative 20–25% estimate for full automation within four years, but does not state that technological base rates imply a substantial probability within the next century.

astra-6.text:
I think the outside view should make you pretty skeptical of confident claims here. Four years is a short time to go from systems that are useful for parts of the work to systems that can run an entire AI company. And historically, automating an occupation has often been much harder than automating a bunch of the tasks within it.

But I’m also skeptical of using that as a decisive argument. The relevant question is whether AI can automate the research and engineering that produces better AI. If it can, then the rate of progress could change substantially, and extrapolating from how long previous technologies took to diffuse might be misleading.

I’d also distinguish between automating essentially all the technical work and literally having no humans involved. You could still have humans making decisions, signing contracts, or providing oversight while AI does almost all the work that determines how quickly the company advances. That seems like the more relevant threshold.

So I’d use outside-view reasoning to temper confidence, but put substantial weight on the specific capabilities these systems have, how quickly those capabilities are improving, and what obstacles remain to doing long, complicated projects autonomously. I don’t think the outside view by itself settles whether that happens within four years.

r001.rationale: It calls four years a short time to progress from partial task automation to running an entire AI company, and says the outside view should make confident claims less likely.

r002.rationale: It gives no estimate of the probability of full automation within the next century and does not say naive technological base rates imply a substantial chance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the outside view is a useful sanity check, but I don’t think it should dominate here. If you look at how long it normally takes to automate an industry, four years sounds implausibly fast. But a lot of that history involves automating physical tasks or deploying systems across many different organisations. Automating the work inside an AI company is a somewhat different proposition.

The question I’d put more weight on is: what can the models do now, what are the remaining obstacles, and how quickly should we expect those obstacles to fall? You also have this possibility that better models accelerate AI research, which produces better models. That makes extrapolating from the usual pace of organisational change less reliable.

That said, “fully automated” is a pretty strong claim. Being able to automate most research and engineering work is different from reliably running the whole company without humans. So I’d take the outside view as a reason to be sceptical of the strongest version, while still taking very substantial automation within four years seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says four years sounds implausibly fast based on how long industry automation normally takes, and treats that as a reason to doubt the strongest full-automation claim.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that a naive outside-view analysis gives a substantial probability of full automation within the next century.
